title: HVR-Met: A Hypothesis-Verification-Replanning Agentic System for Extreme Weather Diagnosis
one_liner: Diagnose extreme weather with an agent loop that proposes a cause, checks it against evidence, and replans when the evidence disagrees.
lead: Weather forecasting tells us what may happen next, but diagnosis asks why a dangerous event is forming and which signals support that explanation. That task is hard because the agent must combine many evidence sources, domain knowledge, and multi-step reasoning. HVR-Met builds a meteorology-focused multi-agent system around a closed loop: form a hypothesis, verify it against evidence, and replan if the check fails.

problem.h2: Why extreme weather diagnosis is harder than ordinary prediction
paras: Extreme weather diagnosis requires more than detecting a pattern in data. A useful diagnosis must connect observed signals to a causal story about pressure systems, moisture transport, instability, timing, and location. That demands iterative reasoning because one candidate explanation may fit one signal and fail on another.

Generic agents struggle here because they often lack domain-specific checking routines and because simple one-pass reasoning does not support repeated correction. HVR-Met addresses this by building a dedicated loop that keeps testing candidate explanations against meteorological evidence.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Turn weather diagnosis into a repeated cycle of propose, verify, and replan so that the system can correct wrong explanations before reaching a final conclusion.

panels.title: 1. Warning signs appear
panels.viz_args: Satellite, radar, pressure, moisture, and wind signals arrive
panels.caption: The system sees many clues, but those clues do not yet explain the event.

panels.title: 2. First explanation is proposed
panels.viz_args: Hypothesis: event driven mainly by moisture surge and local uplift
panels.caption: A candidate diagnosis gives the system something concrete to test.

panels.title: 3. Verification stage checks evidence
panels.caption: The system checks whether each important signal agrees with the current explanation.

panels.title: 4. Replanning updates the diagnosis
panels.caption: Failed checks lead to a new hypothesis rather than a forced answer.

panels.title: 5. Final diagnosis survives checks
panels.caption: The answer is stronger because it passed repeated verification against domain evidence.

steps.text: Gather the meteorological signals needed to explain an extreme event rather than only predict it.
Use expert knowledge and agent reasoning to propose a candidate explanation for the event.
Check whether the proposed explanation matches fine-grained evidence across sub-tasks and time steps.
Revise the hypothesis and choose new evidence-gathering or reasoning steps because the current story is incomplete.
Measure whether the system handles the small reasoning steps well enough to support the final diagnosis.

paras: The paper changes the reasoning loop used for weather diagnosis. Instead of a one-shot answer, it inserts explicit verification and replanning stages grounded in expert knowledge.
object.object: The control loop for domain-specific diagnosis

hidden.name: How well a candidate weather explanation matches all relevant evidence at once
paras: The central hidden quantity is hypothesis validity. A candidate explanation can match some signals while failing others, so the system must estimate whether the whole story is still coherent enough to keep or whether it should be revised.

This quantity is hidden because no single measurement directly says the current explanation is right. The agent must aggregate support and contradiction across many checks. HVR-Met uses verification and replanning to repeatedly sharpen that estimate.

heat.caption: High values mark the places where the system most needs to judge whether its current explanation still holds together.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether the current explanation really fits the full set of weather evidence well enough to trust.
The hypothesis-verification-replanning loop keeps updating this quantity by checking each explanation against expert-guided evidence and revising when contradictions remain.

paras: Explicit verification helps because complex diagnosis is rarely solved in one pass. A first explanation may be partly right, but a structured checking stage can expose where it fails, which gives the system a concrete target for revision.

Replanning matters because the agent should not treat a failed hypothesis as a final answer. By revising the explanation and testing again, the system can gradually converge on a diagnosis that better fits the evidence. The atomic-level benchmark also helps because it evaluates the small reasoning steps that make the final diagnosis credible.

stages.s: Meteorological evidence for a dangerous event
Verify that explanation against detailed evidence

math.words: Score a candidate explanation by how much evidence supports it minus how much evidence contradicts it, and replan when the score falls below a threshold.
math.equation: hypothesis_score = support_total - contradiction_total ; replan when hypothesis_score < threshold
symbols: overall validity score for the current explanation
sum of evidence checks that agree with the explanation
sum of checks that conflict with the explanation
minimum score required to keep the current explanation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an explanation says a storm is driven mainly by moisture transport and local uplift.
Radar structure and moisture indicators support that story, giving support_total = 0.7.
But pressure evolution and timing disagree, giving contradiction_total = 0.5.
If the keep threshold is 0.4, the system must replan because the current explanation leaves too much unresolved conflict.

math.note: The paper's real system is more detailed, but the core logic is direct: keep testing whether the current explanation earns enough support to survive.

charts.title: One-pass weather agent
charts.note: A single pass struggles because it lacks a structured way to correct partial explanations.

charts.title: HVR-Met
charts.note: The loop improves complex cases because failed checks trigger targeted replanning instead of forced completion.

items.b: Bad expert rules can mislead the loop.
items.html: Expert knowledge helps guide reasoning, but weak or outdated rules can steer the system toward the wrong checks because the loop trusts those rules during verification.
Repeated hypothesis revision improves diagnosis, but too many loops can slow the system because each new pass triggers more tool use and more evidence checks.

items.b: Some events may support several plausible stories.
items.html: When multiple explanations fit much of the evidence, the system may remain uncertain because the available signals do not cleanly separate the causes.
Use fine-grained evaluation for intermediate checks and require each final diagnosis to survive explicit evidence tests so that the loop is judged on reasoning quality rather than fluent wording.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a compact event-diagnosis agent for a small weather dataset with interpretable evidence channels such as rainfall, pressure, wind, and moisture. Let the agent propose a cause, score that cause against the evidence, and revise when the score is too low.

The demo should prove that explicit verification improves final diagnosis because the system can detect when its first explanation leaves contradictions unresolved, and that replanning helps most on hard cases where several causes are initially plausible.
demo.metric_eq: loop_gain = diagnosis_score_with_verify_replan - diagnosis_score_one_pass ; recovery_gain = corrected_cases_after_replan - corrected_cases_without_replan
demo.closing: A useful demo shows that a diagnosis loop earns trust by surviving its own checks.
